samples.text:
Most people know that fruit, vegetables and whole grains are good for health, but many of them still eat a lot of junk food. This essay will explain why it is difficult to eat healthily and who should help people to improve their diet.

There are several reasons why people do not eat healthy food. The first reason is time. Many people work long hours and when they come home they are too tired for cooking, so they buy fast food or ready meals which is quick and easy. Secondly, unhealthy food is often cheaper than healthy food. For example, in many supermarket a burger costs less than a salad, so families with low income choose the cheaper option. Another reason is that junk food is very tasty and it is advertised everywhere, so it is difficult to resist it, especially for children.

In my opinion, both the government and individuals should be responsible for this problem. The government can make healthy food cheaper by reducing tax on fruits and vegetables and put higher tax on sugary drinks. They can also teach children about nutrition and cooking at school, so they will have good habits from young age. However, individuals and families also have responsibility, because nobody can force a person to eat well. Parents should cook healthy meals at home and give good example to their children.

In conclusion, people find it hard to eat healthy food because they are busy, healthy food is expensive and junk food is attractive. I believe the government should help by using taxes and education, but people must also take responsibility of their own diet.
samples.why: Answers both questions with a relevant position · reasons and suggestions are sensible but thinly developed · mechanical linking · adequate vocabulary · several errors in articles, agreement and prepositions that do not obscure meaning.

samples.text:
Although most people are well aware that vegetables are healthier than crisps and fizzy drinks, poor diets remain common. This essay will examine why knowledge alone does not lead to healthy eating and argue that responsibility should be shared between governments, the food industry and individuals.

The gap between knowing and doing has several causes. Convenience is a major factor, as people with demanding jobs often lack the time or energy to prepare meals from fresh ingredients after a long day, and processed food offers a quick alternative. Cost also plays an important role. In many places, fresh produce is more expensive than heavily processed snacks, which makes healthy eating difficult for low-income households. Moreover, the modern food environment is designed to encourage overconsumption. Unhealthy products are heavily advertised, placed at eye level in supermarkets and made highly appealing through large amounts of sugar, salt and fat, so even people with good intentions find them hard to resist.

In my view, it would be unfair to place the entire burden on individuals when so many external factors shape their choices. Governments should take a leading role, for example by taxing sugary drinks, subsidising fruit and vegetables and requiring clear nutritional labelling. Schools can also contribute by providing nutritious lunches and teaching practical cooking skills. The food industry has a responsibility too, and manufacturers could be encouraged to reduce the sugar and salt content of their products. Nevertheless, individuals cannot be entirely excused, since they still make the final decision about what they buy, and parents shape children's eating habits from an early age.

In conclusion, people struggle to eat well because of busy lifestyles, the higher cost of healthy food and an environment full of tempting alternatives. Improving diets therefore requires a combined effort in which governments and the food industry makes healthy choices easier and individuals take responsibility for their own decisions.
samples.why: Clear position on shared responsibility · both questions answered with extended support · logical paragraphing and good cohesion · good topic vocabulary (overconsumption, subsidising, fresh produce) · largely accurate with one agreement slip.

samples.text:
It is one of the curiosities of modern life that people can recite the benefits of vegetables and the dangers of sugar, yet still reach for a takeaway at the end of the day. The reasons lie less in ignorance than in the circumstances in which food choices are made, and for this reason I believe responsibility for improving diets must be shared, with governments playing the leading role.

Time pressure is a fundamental obstacle. For people working long hours or juggling several jobs, preparing a balanced meal from scratch can feel like an unrealistic demand, whereas ready meals and fast food require no effort at all. Price reinforces this pattern: calorie for calorie, processed food is often cheaper than fresh produce, so households on tight budgets may have little real choice. Perhaps most importantly, the food environment itself works against good intentions. Products high in sugar, salt and fat are engineered to be highly palatable, promoted relentlessly and positioned prominently in shops, which means that choosing the healthy option requires constant willpower. Knowledge, in other words, is rarely a match for convenience, cost and temptation combined.

Given these pressures, it would be unrealistic to expect individuals to solve the problem alone. Governments are best placed to reshape the environment in which choices are made, whether through taxes on sugary drinks, subsidies for fresh produce, restrictions on junk-food advertising or clear front-of-pack labelling. Food manufacturers should also be held accountable, for instance through targets to reduce harmful ingredients. Schools have a role in teaching cooking and providing nutritious meals, thereby shaping habits early. Individuals, of course, retain ultimate control over what they eat, but personal responsibility is far easier to exercise when the healthy choice is also the easy one.

In conclusion, poor diets persist because of time pressure, cost and a food environment designed to tempt. While individuals must play their part, governments, supported by industry and schools, should take the lead in making healthy eating affordable and convenient.
samples.why: Both questions fully answered with a clear, well-justified position · ideas extended and logically linked · wide, natural vocabulary (palatable, calorie for calorie, accountable) · wide range of structures with no errors.
